questions.question: A 65-year-old HIV-positive man presented with fever and breathlessness for 2 weeks. Imaging shows dense infiltration in the lower lobe, and the lung biopsy showed the following findings. What is the diagnosis?

explanation.text: The patient's presentation with fever and breathlessness for 2 weeks and history of HIV with owl eye appearance in the image is suggestive of CMV pneumonia.
Incorrect Options: Options A, C, and D do not have an owl eye appearance.

questions.question: A 28-year-old female presents with a painless, bluish, fluctuant and translucent swelling on the lower lip that enlarges with eating or pressure, as shown in the image below. She reports a history of accidentally biting her lip frequently. What histopathological feature would be expected on biopsy of the lesion?

options.A: Mucin-filled cavity surroundedby granulation tissue and chronic inflammatory cells.
options.B: Proliferation of ductal cells within fibrous connective tissue
options.D: Eosinophilic granuloma with multinucleated giant cells

explanation.text: The clinical presentation and the image suggest Mucocele, a benign cystic lesion caused by the accumulation of saliva due to trauma or obstruction of the salivary gland duct. Histologically, it is characterized by a mucin-filled cavity without an epithelial lining (in the extravasation type), surrounded by granulation tissue and chronic inflammatory cells, especially macrophages (mucinophages).

Mucin-filled cavity incites an inflammatory response, and for the repair of this, the body will start making granulation tissue. A mucocele is an extravasation cyst: Due to excessive lip biting or any trauma, accumulation of lots of saliva and mucus occurs, resulting in a cystic lesion. It does not have any ductal epithelium or ductal lining. A t rue cyst lined by ductal epithelium.
Treatment: Cryotherapy Laser Treatment Surgical Excision: Removal of the cyst

questions.question: A 40-year-old female presents with a slowly growing painless mass in her left parotid gland region that has been present for several months. On examination, a firm, mobile, non-tender mass is palpable in the preauricular area. Fine needle aspiration cytology (FNAC) reveals epithelial and myoepithelial cells in a chondromyxoid background. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanation.text: Type of tumour Nature of the tumour HPE features Pleomorphic adenoma Benign mixed tumor Commonly seen in the parotid gland. More common in females Mixed tumor with epithelial and mesenchymal components.

Epithelial component: Cells Mesenchymal component: Chondromyxoid stroma Warthin tumour (Option B) Benign Oncocytic cells with double-layered lining Mucoepidermoid carcinoma (Option C) Low to intermediate malignant potential Mucinous and squamous epithelial cells, variable cystic spaces Adenoid cystic carcinoma (Option D) Intermediate to high-grade malignant Cribriform pattern, perineural invasion

questions.question: A 45-year-old female presents with a painless, slowly growing mass in her left parotid gland. Examination reveals a firm, mobile mass. Biopsy confirms pleomorphic adenoma with characteristic islands of cartilage and foci of bone in a myxoid stroma. Which of the following is incorrect regarding this condition?

options.A: Mostly found in the parotid gland
options.B: Mixed tumours with ductal, myoepithelial and mesenchymal cells
options.C: Radiation exposure is a risk factor
options.D: Down-regulation of PLAG1 results in abnormal cell proliferation

explanation.text: Pleomorphic adenoma is a benign mixed tumor predominantly of the parotid gland and is commonly seen in females. It contains both epithelial (ductal and myoepithelial) and mesenchymal components (myxoid, chondroid, and osseous tissue). Radiation exposure is a known risk factor for salivary gland tumors, including pleomorphic adenoma.

The PLAG1 (PLAG= Pleomorphic Adenoma Gene) gene is an oncogene, and up-regulation or overexpression (not down-regulation) of PLAG1 leads to abnormal cell proliferation and tumorigenesis in pleomorphic adenoma.

questions.question: A 55-year-old male has a painless, slowly enlarging mass in the left parotid gland over several years. Examination reveals a firm, mobile, non-tender mass. Histological findings confirm pleomorphic adenoma. Which factor is associated with an increased risk of malignant transformation in pleomorphic adenomas?

options.D: Presence of hyalinized stroma within the tumour

explanation.text: Rates of malignant transformation in pleomorphic adenoma correlate with the age of the lesion When the age of pleomorphic adenoma's lesion exceeds 15-20 years, the chances of malignant transformations increase: Carcinoma ex pleomorphic adenoma (Carcinoma has originated inside a pre-existing pleomorphic adenoma). Pleomorphic adenoma It is a benign mixed tumor Most common salivary gland tumor and most commonly occurs in the parotid.

Mostly seen in females. On FNAC or biopsy: It shows epithelial and mesenchymal cells (mixed tumor) Epithelial components: Epithelia, myoepithelial and ductal cells Mesenchymal tissue comprise of chondromyxoid stroma

questions.question: A 50-year-old male smoker presents with a painless swelling in the parotid region. Fine needle aspiration cytology (FNAC) reveals murky fluid. Which of the following histopathological features is true regarding this condition?

options.A: Proliferation of squamous epithelial cells with keratinisation

explanation.text: The clinical presentation (history of chronic smoking) and histopathological image (Murky fluid on FNAC) suggest a Warthin tumour or Papillary cystadenoma lymphomatosum, a benign salivary gland tumour that typically occurs in the parotid gland. On histopathology i t is characterised by: Pink coloured oncocytic cells, which are double-layered. Deep blue coloured lymphocytes.

Papillary cystadenoma lymphomatosum: Papillary: Shows papillary projections Cyst: Cyst which is filled with murky fluid which is aspirated on FNAC. Adenoma: Because it is a benign tumor Lymphomatosum: It contains significant lymphoid components. It is seen in chronic smokers and commonly involves bilateral parotid glands.
This characteristic appearance is often referred to as "Cystic oncocytic hyperplasia." Proliferation of squamous epithelial cells with keratinisation (Option A): Seen in pleomorphic adenoma

questions.question: Which of the following statements about Warthin's tumour is true?

options.A: It is the most common malignant tumour of the salivary glands.
options.B: They are typically located in the parotid gland.
options.C: It is more common in females.

explanation.text: Warthin tumour or Papillary cystadenoma lymphomatosum is a benign salivary gland tumour primarily affecting the parotid gland. It is more common in males and is strongly associated with a history of smoking. Parotid involvement can be bilateral. On FNAC, Murky fluid is aspirated. Histopathological features: Shows papillary projections It is a benign tumour with cyst formation.
Cells: Double-layered pink-coloured oncocytic cells and a lot of lymphocytic infiltrates.

**It is the most common malignant tumour of the salivary glands (Option A):** Warthin tumour is a benign tumour It is more common in females (Option C): It is more common in males, especially with a history of smoking.
**Associated with human papillomavirus (HPV) infection (Option D):** It is associated with heavy chronic smoking.

questions.question: A 45-year-old female presents with a slow-growing painless mass in the left submandibular gland region. Imaging studies reveal a solid lesion with cystic components. Fine needle aspiration cytology (FNAC) shows a mixture of mucin-producing, epidermoid, and intermediate cells. A histopathology image is given below. Which of the following features is true regarding this condition?

options.A: Most commonly found in the sublingual salivary glands.
options.B: Most are associated with a (11;19) translocation.
options.D: Histologically characterized by the presence of spindle cells

explanation.text: Mucoepidermoid carcinoma (MEC): It is the most common malignant tumour of salivary glands, often found in parotid and submandibular glands. ( Option A) It does not have a capsule ( Option C) It is associated with the (11;19) chromosomal translocation, creating CRTC1-MAML2 fusion protein.

Histologically, it exhibits squamous and mucous cell features. (Option D) There are 3 types of cells in Mucoepidermoid carcinoma: Mucus-producing cells Epidermoid or Squamoid cells Intermediate cells. Grading: Low grade MEC: If mucus component is predominant. High grade MEC: If epidermoid or squamoid component is predominant. Image: Low-power view showing sheets and micro cysts containing cells of varying morphologies in Mucoepidermoid Carcinoma.

questions.question: A 55-year-old male presents with a slowly enlarging painless mass in the right parotid gland region. Imaging studies reveal a solid tumour with a characteristic "Swiss cheese" appearance on MRI. Fine needle aspiration cytology (FNAC) shows basaloid cells with cribriform and tubular patterns. Which of the following statements is true regarding this condition?

options.A: Most commonly occur in the parotid and submandibular glands.
options.B: MYB-NFIB gene rearrangements are present in all cases
options.C: Encapsulated lesions with a smooth surface.
options.D: Tend to grow rapidly and have a high mitotic rate.

explanation.text: The clinical presentation and characteristic ‘Swiss cheese’ appearance on MRI with basaloid cells and cribriform pattern on FNAC suggest Adenoid cystic carcinoma, which most commonly affects parotid and submandibular glands. Cribriform pattern in a salivary gland tumor always tells us about Adenoid Cystic Carcinoma.
**MYB-NFIB gene rearrangements are present in all cases (Option B):** MYB-NFIB gene rearrangements are present in a subset of adenoid cystic carcinomas and not in all cases.

**Encapsulated lesions with a smooth surface (Option C):** It is poorly capsulated Tend to grow rapidly and have a high mitotic rate (Option D) Adenoid cystic carcinomas are slow-growing tumours that tend to invade perineural spaces (therefore painful lesions), indicating a low mitotic rate. Image: Three typical growth patterns, including cribriform (left), tubular (center), and solid (right).

questions.question: Warthin's tumor is also called?

explanation.text: Warthin's tumor is also known as adenolymphoma. It's a benign tumor that most commonly occurs in the parotid gland, which is a salivary gland located in the cheek. It's characterized by its unique histological appearance, with cystic spaces and papillary projections lined by double-layered oncocytic epithelial cells and lymphoid stroma.

Incorrect Options: Option B - Pleomorphic Adenoma: Pleomorphic adenoma is another type of salivary gland tumor. It is the most common type of salivary gland tumor, but it is distinct from Warthin's tumor. Pleomorphic adenoma is characterized by a mixture of epithelial and myoepithelial cells in a chondromyxoid stroma.

Option C - Mucoepidermoid Carcinoma: Mucoepidermoid carcinoma is a malignant salivary gland tumor. It is not synonymous with Warthin's tumor. Mucoepidermoid carcinoma is characterized by a combination of mucous-secreting, epidermoid (squamous), and intermediate cells. It is one of the most common malignant salivary gland tumors.

Option D - Acinic Cell Carcinoma: Acinic cell carcinoma is another type of malignant salivary gland tumor. It is characterized by the presence of acinar cells, which produce serous (watery) secretions. It is not the same as Warthin's tumor.

questions.question: Which of the following features is not observed in pleomorphic adenoma?

explanation.text: Perineural invasion is not observed in pleomorphic adenoma, as it is a benign tumour. Perineural invasion occurs in carcinoma ex pleomorphic adenoma, a malignant transformation of pleomorphic adenoma. Pleomorphic Adenoma: Most common salivary gland neoplasm: Represents ~60% of parotid tumours, less common in submandibular and minor salivary glands.

Benign tumour: Composed of ductal (epithelial), myoepithelial, and mesenchymal cells (also called mixed tumour). Risk factors: Radiation exposure increases risk. Chromosomal rearrangements, including overexpression of PLAG1 and mutations in HMGA2, are commonly associated. Clinical presentation: Painless, slow-growing, mobile, discrete masses, usually in the parotid, submandibular, or buccal cavity.

Recurrence: 4% recurrence rate after parotidectomy; 25% after simple enucleation due to tumour extension beyond the capsule. Malignant transformation: Occurs more often with the age of the lesion. 2% of tumours present <5 years develop malignancy; 10% present >15 years develop malignancy, usually adenocarcinomas or undifferentiated carcinomas.

Aggressive cancers: If malignant transformation occurs, cancers are highly infiltrative, with a 30-50% mortality rate at 5 years. Morphology: Size: Typically rounded, well-demarcated masses <6 cm. Histological features: Heterogeneous morphology with ductal, acinar, tubule-like structures, and myoepithelial cells (Option A).

**Background of myxoid, hyaline, and chondroid stroma (Option C):** (cartilage-like areas). Rare bone foci. No significant epithelial dysplasia or mitotic activity. Tumour behaviour: Similar clinical course regardless of whether epithelial or mesenchymal elements dominate.
**Keratin pearls (Option B):** While rare, keratin pearls can occasionally be observed in pleomorphic adenoma, especially when there is squamous metaplasia within the tumour.

questions.question: A middle-aged woman presents with dry eyes and dry mouth. Laboratory tests reveal positive anti-Ro (SSA) and anti-La (SSB) antibodies. What is the most likely underlying pathological mechanism?

options.A: Destruction of exocrine glands by neutrophils
options.C: Lymphocytic infiltration and destruction of salivary and lacrimal glands
options.D: Deposition of amyloid in salivary glands

explanation.text: This presentation is classic for Sjögren’s syndrome, an autoimmune disorder characterised by chronic lymphocytic infiltration of the salivary and lacrimal glands, leading to xerostomia (dry mouth) and keratoconjunctivitis sicca (dry eyes). The condition is most common in middle-aged women and is associated with anti-Ro (SSA) and anti-La (SSB) autoantibodies. Pathophysiology Epithelial cells aS active players.

Salivary/lacrimal epithelial cells (the target tissue) can act like antigen-presenting cells under stress or after viral/other triggers. They upregulate type I interferons, express costimulatory molecules and release chemokines that recruit lymphocytes. Autoantigen exposure. Apoptosis or other epithelial injury exposes intracellular ribonucleoproteins (Ro/SSA, La/SSB) to the immune system, promoting an autoimmune response.

T-cell-driven inflammation. Early lesions are dominated by CD4⁺ T cells that home to the glands and cause inflammation and cytokine release (TH1/TH17 pathways are implicated). B-cell activation & ectopic germinal centres. Chronic inflammation induces local B-cell activation, formation of ectopic germinal–centre–like structures within glands, and production of autoantibodies (anti-Ro/SSA, anti-La/SSB, rheumatoid factor).

Elevated BAFF (B-cell activating factor) supports B-cell survival. Structural loss of secretory tissue. Progressive acinar atrophy, ductal dilation and replacement by lymphoid infiltrates/fibrosis → functional loss of saliva and tears.
**Incorrect Options: Destruction of exocrine glands by neutrophils (Option A):** is more typical of suppurative infections, not autoimmune Sjögren’s.
**IgE-mediated hypersensitivity reaction (Option B):** occurs in allergies and anaphylaxis, not in this chronic autoimmune process.
**Deposition of amyloid in salivary glands (Option D):** can occur in systemic amyloidosis, but is not the main mechanism in Sjögren’s syndrome.

questions.question: A 58-year-old male presents with chronic heartburn and regurgitation. Upper endoscopy reveals the presence of Barrett's esophagus. What is the primary cellular change seen in this condition?

explanation.text: The primary cellular change seen in Barrett's oesophagus is metaplasia of squamous epithelium into intestinal columnar epithelium because of acid reflux/GERD. Intestinal columnar epithelium has goblet cells, which are filled with acidic mucin. Acidic mucin is stained by the Alcian blue stain. Metaplasia is 100% reversible. So this metaplasia can be reversed if GERD is controlled with the help of drugs.
If GERD is not controlled, then it can lead to adenocarcinoma of esophagus.

questions.question: A 50-year-old male presents with chronic heartburn for two years. An endoscopy is performed, and the biopsy of the esophageal specimen stained with special stain is shown below. Which of the following conditions is the patient at an increased risk of?

explanation.text: The above scenario and an image showing goblet cells within the columnar epithelium suggest Barret’s esophagus, which puts the patient at an increased risk of adenocarcinoma of the esophagus. Microscopically, the squamous layer is replaced with intestinal-type metaplasia containing goblet cells. Goblet cells are diagnostic of Barrett esophagus and have distinct mucous vacuoles that stain blue with Alcian blue.
Esophageal disease progression: A: Normal esophagus; B: Esophagitis; C: BE with goblet cells; D: Dysplasia; E: EAC. EAC: Esophageal adenocarcinoma; BE: Barrett's esophagus.

questions.question: A woman presented with dysphagia to solids for a month. On examination, there are multiple lesions on the lips. An endoscopy reveals obstructive lesions in the upper oesophagus. Which of the following additional findings can be seen in this patient?

explanation.text: This patient's condition is most likely suggestive of Plummer-Vinson syndrome, which is associated with iron deficiency anemia.

Plummer-Vinson Syndrome (Sideropenic Dysphagia) Characterized by a triad of: Iron-deficiency anemia (Sideropenia) Atrophic glossitis Post- Cricoid Dysphagia (Upper esophageal webs) Common in middle-aged women Increased risk of squamous cell carcinoma (pharynx and proximal esophagus) Post cricoid Dysphagia is caused by esophageal webs/rings in the upper esophagus which leads to swallowing difficulties.

questions.question: A 45-year-old male presents with complaints of severe odynophagia, retrosternal chest pain, and difficulty in swallowing solids and liquids for the past week. He has a history of untreated HIV infection with a CD4 count of 80 cells/mm³. An upper gastrointestinal endoscopy image is shown below. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanation.text: The clinical scenario and endoscopy showing curd-like plaques suggest Candida esophagitis. Candida esophagitis is an opportunistic infection seen in immunocompromised individuals (e.g., HIV/AIDS, cancer patients, long-term corticosteroid therapy or long-term immunosuppressive therapy) CMV esophagitis (Option A): Shallow, linear, or serpiginous ulcers on endoscopy.
**HSV esophagitis (Option B):** Punched-out ulcers on endoscopy Eosinophilic esophagitis (Option C): Seen in patients with allergy and atopy but not associated with immunodeficiency.

questions.question: Which of the following is true regarding the condition shown in the endoscopic image below?

options.C: Interleukin 5 has a major role in pathogenesis.
options.D: Diagnosed by observing at least ten lymphocytes/HPF.

explanation.text: The given image suggests eosinophilic esophagitis, where Interleukin 5 has a major role in pathogenesis.

Eosinophilic Esophagitis: Triggered by allergic reactions to food or environmental allergens (Option A) Associated with atopic dermatitis, allergic rhinitis, asthma, and peripheral eosinophilia Pathophysiology Interleukin 5 (IL-5) key cytokine for eosinophil maturation and activation Clinical Manifestations Dysphagia Epigastric pain Dyspepsia Chest pain Food impaction Diagnostic Criteria Eosinophils ≥ 15 per high power field (HPF) on HPE (Option D) Endoscopic Findings: Stacked circular rings ("feline esophagus") ( Option C) Strictures Linear furrows Characteristic rat tail appearance (Option B)- Rat tail appearance is seen in achalasia cardia.
The characteristic appearance seen in eosinophilic esophagitis on endoscopy is "feline esophagus" which refers to the presence of stacked circular rings.

questions.question: Identify the correct statement/s regarding carcinoma of the oesophagus SCC is more common in the lower two-thirds of the oesophagus Smoking increases the risk of both SCC and adenocarcinoma H. pylori is associated with a decreased risk of oesophageal adenocarcinoma Adenocarcinoma is the overall most common type SCC is linked to fermented milk- mursik, which contains acetaldehyde

Previous radiation to the mediastinum Fermented milk (mursik) containing acetaldehyde Chronic gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) Obesity Smoking Low fruit and vegetable diet Scleroderma p16 and RB gene mutations Protective factor Healthy diet H.pylori- reduces acid, hence reducing GERD. Precursor Lesion None Barrett's oesophagus (metaplasia of squamous to columnar) Histology Keratinisation and pearl formation Glandular differentiation Clinical Presentation Dysphagia, weight loss, chest pain Dysphagia, GERD symptoms, weight loss Prognosis Generally less favourable Generally more favourable

questions.question: A 45 y/o male presents with recurrent episodes of abdominal pain and persistent heartburn. Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy reveals multiple duodenal ulcers. Lab investigations show elevated serum gastrin levels (> 1000 pg/ml). Which features are most likely associated with the patient's condition?

options.A: Presence of gastrin-secreting tumors in the stomach
options.B: Presence of erosive esophagitis and hiatal hernia
options.C: Hyperplasia of parietal cells within the stomach

explanation.text: The characteristic features described in the scenario, including recurrent abdominal pain, heartburn, multiple duodenal ulcers, and elevated serum gastrin levels, strongly suggest a diagnosis of Zollinger-Ellison syndrome. A hallmark feature of Zollinger-Ellison syndrome is marked hyperplasia of parietal cells within the stomach, leading to increased oxyntic mucosal thickness induced by excessive gastrin secretion from gastrinomas.

**Presence of gastrin-secreting tumors in the stomach (Option A):** Zollinger-Ellison syndrome (ZES) is characterized by gastrin-secreting neuroendocrine tumors called gastrinomas. However, these tumors are predominantly found in the small intestine or pancreas rather than the stomach. The most common extrapancreatic site of gastrinoma is the duodenum.

**Presence of erosive esophagitis and hiatal hernia (Option B):** These features are commonly associated with gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD), not Zollinger-Ellison syndrome. ZES primarily presents with duodenal ulcers or chronic diarrhea due to excessive gastric acid secretion from gastrinomas.

**Association with MEN2 gene mutation (Option D):** Gastrinomas are sporadic in 75% of cases. Approximately 25% of patients with gastrinomas have MEN1 (not MEN2), which is linked to aggressive tumor behaviour and primarily presents with duodenal tumors.
